s: 高い授業料を払ったからといって、必ずしも英語が話せるように（　　）。
en: Paying high tuition fees doesn't necessarily mean you'll be able to speak English.
why: 必ずしも locks in a partial denial at the end: 〜とは限らない (or 〜わけではない). からといって points the same way.
〜に違いない is a confident certainty. 必ずしも cannot end in a positive certainty.
〜にきまっている is a gut 'obviously'. 必ずしも needs a negative ending, not a confident one.
〜はずだ is a confident expectation. 必ずしも needs とは限らない or わけではない.
tell: 必ずしも → 〜とは限らない／〜わけではない. Spot it early and skip every positive ending.

s: まさか、あの真面目な田中さんが会社のお金を（　　）。
en: I never dreamed that serious Mr Tanaka had been embezzling company money.
c: 使い込んでいたとは思わなかった
使い込んでいたに違いない
使い込んでいたはずだ
使い込んでいたのは当然だ
why: まさか expresses disbelief and locks in an ending like 〜とは思わなかった or 〜ないだろう.
〜に違いない is confident certainty. It clashes with the shock of まさか.
〜はずだ says it was expected. まさか and 真面目な say the opposite.
〜のは当然だ means 'naturally'. That is the opposite of まさか's disbelief.
tell: まさか → disbelief ending: 〜とは思わなかった／〜ないだろう. Never a confident one.

s: まだ予選なのに、会場は割れるような歓声に包まれ、まるで優勝が（　　）。
en: It was only the qualifying round, yet the arena erupted in deafening cheers, as if the championship had already been won.
c: 決まったかのようだった
決まったに違いなかった
why: まるで locks in a likeness: 〜ようだ／〜みたいだ, often 〜かのようだ ('as if'). The title was not really decided; it only felt that way.
Hearsay そうだ has no past form, and まるで needs a likeness, not a report.
〜らしい is an inference that something is actually true. まるで marks something that only looks like it.
〜に違いない states certainty that it happened. まだ予選 shows it had not.
tell: まるで → 〜ようだ／〜みたいだ (〜かのようだ = as if). Not らしい or そうだ.

s: こんな夜中に、いったい誰が玄関のチャイムを（　　）。
en: Who on earth is ringing the doorbell at this time of night?
c: 鳴らしているのだろう
鳴らしているに違いない
why: いったい + a question word locks in a question ending: 〜のだろう(か) or 〜のか.
〜はずだ is a statement of expectation. いったい誰が needs a question.
〜に違いない is a statement of certainty. You cannot be certain about someone you are asking 'who?' about.
〜ようだ is a statement of how things seem. いったい needs a question ending.
tell: いったい／果たして + question word → 〜のだろう(か)／〜のか.

s: 私はこの計画に反対だ。なぜなら、地元の住民の声が一度も（　　）。
en: I am against this plan, because the local residents have never once been listened to.
c: 聞かれていないからだ
聞かれていないわけがない
聞かれていないに越したことはない
聞かれていないものだ
why: なぜなら opens a reason and locks in 〜から(ため)だ at the end of the sentence.
〜わけがない means 'there's no way'. It gives no reason, and it would deny the very complaint.
〜に越したことはない means 'it's best if'. It turns the complaint into a wish and gives no reason.
〜ものだ states a general truth. なぜなら needs the reason for this objection.
tell: なぜなら／というのは → 〜からだ／〜ためだ at the end.

s: 電車を（　　）、網棚の上に置いた荷物を忘れないように気をつけてください。
en: When you get off the train, be careful not to forget any luggage you put on the overhead rack.
why: Inner-clause tense follows the order of events. You take your luggage BEFORE stepping off, so the inner verb stays in dictionary form: 降りるとき.
降りたとき = once you are off the train. By then the luggage is already left behind.
〜てから = after getting off. Too late to take the luggage down from the rack.
〜たあとで = after getting off. Same problem: the luggage is still on the train.
cue: 網棚の上に置いた荷物
tell: Inner event comes AFTER the main one → dictionary form (降りるとき = just before getting off).

s: 先月、久しぶりに北海道の実家に（　　）、父の髪がすっかり白くなっていて驚いた。
en: Last month, when I went back to my parents' home in Hokkaido for the first time in ages, I was surprised to find my father's hair had gone completely white.
why: I could only see my father's hair once I had arrived home. The inner event comes first, so it takes た形: 帰ったとき.
帰るとき = while setting off or still on the way. My father was at the house, so I could not have seen him yet.
帰る前に = before the trip home. I saw my father after arriving, not before leaving.
〜ようとしたとき = just as I was about to set off. Still before the trip, so I could not have seen him.
tell: Main event happens after arrival (seeing Dad at home) → た形 + とき. 〜るとき = still on the way.

s: この薬は、食事を（　　）あとで、コップ一杯の水と一緒に飲んでください。
en: Take this medicine after your meal, with a glass of water.
why: あと always takes た形, even about the future: the meal is done first, then the medicine.
Dictionary form goes with 前 (食事をする前に), not with あと.
している means during the meal. あと needs the meal to be finished.
しないあとで makes no sense: you cannot be 'after not eating'.
tell: 〜たあと(で) always, even for the future. 〜る前(に) always, even for the past.

s: 来週の会議で（　　）資料は、前日までに全員に配っておいてください。
en: Please hand out the materials for next week's meeting to everyone by the day before.
why: The handout goes out first and the meeting uses it later. The inner event comes after the main one, so dictionary form: 使う資料.
使った would mean the meeting had already used them. Then they could not be handed out the day before.
使っていた describes use going on in the past. Next week's meeting has not happened yet.
使ってきた means 'have been using up to now'. A meeting next week has no history yet.
tell: Noun-modifying clause: tense follows order of events. Used later than the main action → る形.

s: 駅に（　　）、すぐに電話をください。車で迎えに行きますから。
en: As soon as you get to the station, give me a call. I'll come and pick you up by car.
why: The main clause is a request (〜ください). たら accepts a request, wish or intention, and it means 'once you've arrived'.
と cannot be followed by a request, wish or intention. It is for natural, automatic results.
ば after an action verb cannot be followed by a request. 着けば、電話をください is unnatural.
〜ても means 'even if'. 'Even if you arrive, call me' makes no sense.
tell: Request, wish or 〜よう after the condition → たら (or なら). と and ば are out.

s: A「コンサートのチケット、もう買ったよ。」B「もう（　　）、当日は早めに会場に行ったほうがいいよ。グッズ売り場がかなり混むらしいから。」
en: A: "I've already bought the concert ticket." B: "If you've already bought it, you'd better get to the venue early on the day. The merch stand gets really crowded, apparently."
why: The ticket is already bought, so this is a known fact (確定). For something already done, なら becomes 〜たのなら.
買うなら means 'if you are going to buy'. It treats the purchase as not done yet, but A has already bought it.
ば is hypothetical and cannot take advice after an action verb. It also clashes with もう.
と cannot be followed by advice (ほうがいい), and it treats buying as a general condition.
tell: Already happened + advice → 〜たのなら. 〜るなら treats it as not done yet.

s: 秋に京都へ（　　）、ホテルは早めに予約しておいたほうがいいですよ。紅葉の時期はすぐに満室になりますから。
en: If you're going to Kyoto in autumn, you'd better book a hotel early. Everywhere fills up in the autumn-leaves season.
why: なら takes up the listener's plan and gives advice to act on BEFORE it happens. You book the hotel before the trip, so 行くなら.
行ったら = once you have arrived. Booking early has to happen before the trip, so たら puts the events in the wrong order.
ば after an action verb cannot take advice like 〜ほうがいい, and it also puts the trip before the booking.
と marks an automatic result and cannot be followed by advice like 〜ほうがいい.
tell: Advice to act on before the plan (book, prepare, check) → 〜るなら. 〜たら puts the plan first.

s: どんなに（　　）、試験が終わるまではゲームは我慢しよう。
en: However much I want to play games, I'll hold off until the exams are over.
why: どんなに pairs with 〜ても, and 〜ても can be followed by the speaker's will (我慢しよう).
のに cannot be followed by the speaker's will or intention. With 〜しよう, use ても.
やりたければ means 'if you want to play'. That points toward playing, the opposite of 我慢しよう, and どんなに needs ても.
と cannot be followed by the speaker's will, and どんなに needs ても.
tell: どんなに → 〜ても. のに refuses the speaker's will; ても accepts it.

s: 旅行先の駅で、私はうっかりカメラ（　　）、そのまま気づかずにホテルへ戻ってしまった。
en: At a station on my trip, I carelessly dropped my camera and went back to the hotel without noticing.
why: うっかり marks my own carelessness, so use the transitive: カメラを落とした = I dropped it, my fault. A sequence 〜て also keeps the same subject (私) on both sides.
が落ちて focuses on the camera falling by itself. It hides whose fault it was, and the subject would jump from the camera to 私 across a sequence 〜て.
を落とされて is a suffering passive: someone else dropped it on me. うっかり says the carelessness was mine.
が落とされて makes the camera the target of someone else's action. That clashes with 私は and うっかり.
tell: Own carelessness (うっかり・つい) → 他動詞 (〜を落とした). Same subject across a sequence 〜て.

s: コーヒーのしみを洗剤でいくらこすっても、（　　）。
en: However hard I scrubbed the coffee stain with detergent, it wouldn't come out.
why: The result of an attempt goes with the intransitive: I tried, but the stain did not come out (落ちなかった).
落とさなかった means I chose not to remove it. That contradicts いくらこすっても.
落とされなかった is passive: it was not removed by someone. Nobody else is acting here.
落とさせなかった is causative: I did not let someone remove it. Nobody else is involved.
tell: Tried hard, it didn't work → 自動詞 for the result (落ちなかった・開かなかった).

s: 風もないのに、閉めたはずの窓がひとりでに（　　）。
en: Even though there was no wind, the window I was sure I had shut opened by itself.
why: ひとりでに ('by itself') means no one did it. The change of the thing itself takes the intransitive: 窓が開いた.
開ける is transitive and needs someone doing it. ひとりでに rules that out, and 窓が does not fit a transitive verb.
開けられた is passive: someone opened it. That contradicts ひとりでに.
開かせた is causative: someone made it open. ひとりでに rules out any causer.
tell: No doer (ひとりでに・自然に) → 自動詞 (窓が開いた).

s: A「どうしたの？」B「このジャムの瓶、ふたが固くてなかなか（　　）んだ。ちょっと開けてくれない？」
en: A: "What's up?" B: "The lid on this jam jar is so tight it just won't open. Could you open it for me?"
why: The intransitive negative works as a potential: the lid won't open. ふたが + あかない is the natural way to say something won't budge.
あけない is transitive and means I am choosing not to open it. B is asking for help, so B wants it open.
あけさせない is causative: the lid won't let anyone open it. A lid cannot give or refuse permission.
あけていない means I haven't opened it yet. It reports what I did, not that the lid is stuck, and ふたが needs an intransitive.
tell: Won't budge (ふたが・ドアが) → 自動詞 negative as a potential: あかない.

s: 少子化が進むなか、この町の小学校の児童数は、今後さらに（　　）だろう。
en: With the birth rate falling, the number of pupils at this town's primary schools is likely to drop even further from now on.
why: 〜ていく = a change moving away from now into the future. 今後 + だろう fix the time as 'from now on'.
減ってきた = a change up to now. 今後 points forward.
減っていった = a change that went on in the past. 今後 points forward.
減ってきている = a change running up to the present. It cannot describe what happens 今後.
tell: 今後・これから → 〜ていく. 今まで・ずっと → 〜てきた.

s: この店は創業以来100年間、ずっと同じ味を（　　）。
en: Ever since it was founded a hundred years ago, this shop has kept the same flavour.
why: 以来 = from a past point up to now. 〜てきた brings a continuing action up to the speaker's present.
〜ていく points from now into the future. 以来 looks back from the past to now.
〜ていった is a past change moving away. 以来 needs a line that reaches now.
〜てくる (non-past) describes something from now on. A hundred years up to now needs 〜てきた.
tell: 以来・今まで・ずっと (past up to now) → 〜てきた.

s: 会議が終わると、社員たちは一人また一人と会議室を（　　）、最後には私と部長だけが残った。
en: When the meeting ended, the staff left the meeting room one after another, until only the manager and I remained.
why: The speaker stays inside the room (私と部長だけが残った). People leaving move away from the speaker: 出ていく.
出てくる = come out toward the speaker, which puts the speaker outside the room. But 私 stayed inside.
入っていく = go into the room. The meeting has ended and people are leaving.
入ってくる = come into the room toward the speaker. People were leaving, not arriving.
cue: 私と部長だけが残った
tell: Find the speaker. Inside, people leave → 〜ていく. Outside, people come out → 〜てくる.

s: 台所のほうから、カレーのおいしそうなにおいが（　　）。
en: A delicious smell of curry came drifting from the kitchen.
why: A smell or sound reaching the speaker moves toward them: 〜てくる. においがしてきた = a smell came to me.
〜ていく moves away from the speaker. A smell you notice is arriving, not leaving.
させてきた is causative: someone made the smell. においが is the subject, so there is no causer.
されてきた is passive. においがする is not something done to the smell.
tell: Smells, sounds, feelings reaching you → 〜てくる (においがしてきた・聞こえてきた).

s: 戦争を生き抜いた祖父の話に、平和とは何かを改めて（　　）。
en: My grandfather's story of surviving the war made me think afresh about what peace really is.
why: Causative-passive 〜させられた = something moved me to think. The story, marked with に, is the cause, and I am the thinker. Very common in essays.
考えさせた is causative: I made someone think. There is nobody here for me to make think.
考えられた is passive or potential. 'Was thought by the story' or 'was able to think' does not fit 話に as the cause.
考えた is plain active. It cannot take the cause with に (話に考えた is wrong).
tell: Cause + に + a thought that rose in me → 〜させられた (考えさせられた・反省させられた).

s: 新人のころは、毎朝誰よりも早く出社して、先輩たちの机を（　　）ものだ。
en: When I was new, I used to come in before anyone else every morning and was made to wipe down the senior staff's desks.
why: As the newcomer, I was made to do it: causative-passive 拭かされた. 〜たものだ looks back on a past habit.
拭かせた = I made someone else wipe. The newcomer who comes in earliest is the one doing the chore.
拭かれた is passive: the desks were wiped, or someone wiped them on me. It loses the point that I did the wiping.
拭いてもらった = someone wiped for me. But I came in early to do it myself.
tell: Made to do it by people above you → causative-passive 〜させられる (拭かされた).

s: 徹夜で仕上げたレポートの上に、弟にコーヒーを（　　）、一から書き直すはめになった。
en: My little brother spilled coffee all over the report I'd stayed up all night finishing, and I ended up having to rewrite it from scratch.
why: The speaker suffered from someone else's action: passive with the doer marked by に (弟にこぼされて). はめになった confirms the harm.
こぼさせて is causative: I made my brother spill it. Nobody makes someone ruin their own report.
こぼして is active: I spilled it. Then 弟に has no role.
こぼれて is intransitive and cannot take コーヒーを. It also hides who did it.
tell: Someone else's act harms you → passive (Xに〜される). はめになる confirms it.

s: 子どもが自分で選んだ道なら、親としては好きなように（　　）と思う。
en: If it's a path my child chose for themselves, as a parent I want to let them do it their own way.
why: Causative of permission (〜させる) + 〜てやる: the parent lets the child do it. 子どもが自分で選んだ道 shows the child is the one acting.
やらされたい = want to be made to do it. The parent is not the one being pushed.
やってあげたい = the parent wants to do it for the child. But it is the child's own path.
やられたい is passive: want to have it done to me. That makes no sense here.
cue: 子どもが自分で選んだ道
tell: Letting someone do it (permission) → 〜させる (やらせてやる). 〜てあげる means you do it yourself.

s: せっかくの休日なのに、朝6時に上司からの電話で（　　）。
en: It was my precious day off, but I was woken at 6 a.m. by a call from my boss.
why: An unwelcome act done to the speaker takes the passive. せっかくの休日なのに shows it was unwanted.
〜てもらった = a favour I wanted. A 6 a.m. call on a day off is not one.
〜てくれた = someone kindly did it for me. It clashes with なのに.
〜てあげた = I did it for someone. The call woke me, not the other way round.
cue: せっかくの休日なのに
tell: Unwelcome → passive (起こされた). Welcome → 〜てもらった／〜てくれた.

s: 引っ越しのとき、大学時代の友人が二人も手伝いに来て（　　）、予定より早く終わった。
en: When I moved house, two of my old university friends came to help, so we finished earlier than planned.
why: 友人が is the subject and the speaker receives the help. Giver as subject, me as receiver → 〜てくれる.
〜てもらう needs the receiver (me) as subject and the giver with に (友人に来てもらって). Here 友人が is the subject.
〜てあげる sends the favour away from the speaker. Friends helping me move comes toward me.
〜ていただく is the humble もらう: it needs 友人に, not 友人が, and it is far too formal for your own friends in a plain-style account.
tell: Xが + a favour for me → 〜てくれる. Xに + a favour for me → 〜てもらう.

s: いとこの由美は、近所に住む大学の先生に頼んで、自分の書いた英語の作文を（　　）そうだ。
en: I hear my cousin Yumi asked a university professor who lives nearby to look over an English essay she had written.
why: 由美 is closer to the speaker than the professor, so she is the subject. She asked and received the favour: 先生に見てもらった.
〜てあげた = 由美 did a favour for the professor. But it is her own essay and she asked for help.
〜てくれた needs the giver as subject and the speaker's side receiving. 由美は is the subject, so she would be the giver.
見られた (passive) would mean the reading was unwanted. 頼んで shows she wanted it.
tell: Person closer to you as subject + 頼んで → 〜てもらう. Passive would mean it was unwanted.

s: 寝ぐせのついた頭のまま歩いていたら、同僚に写真を（　　）、社内のチャットに載せられてしまった。
en: I was walking around with bed hair, and a colleague snapped a photo of me and posted it in the company chat.
why: An unwelcome act by someone else takes the passive: 同僚に撮られて. 載せられてしまった confirms it.
〜てもらって = a favour I asked for. Nobody asks to be photographed with bed hair.
〜てくれて = someone kindly did it for me. It clashes with 載せられてしまった.
〜てあげて = I did it for the colleague. The colleague took the photo, not me.
tell: Same act, opposite feeling: unwelcome → 〜られる; welcome → 〜てもらう.

s: 部長、来月の新商品発表会の司会ですが、ぜひ私に（　　）。
en: About hosting next month's new product launch: would you please let me take it on?
c: 担当させていただけないでしょうか
担当していただけないでしょうか
担当させてあげられないでしょうか
担当してもよろしいでしょうか
why: I want to do it and need the manager's permission: causative (let me do it) + いただけないでしょうか. 私に marks me as the one who will do it.
担当していただけないでしょうか asks the manager to take it on himself. ぜひ私に shows I want the job.
〜てあげる sends a favour away from the speaker, as when you plead for someone else (彼に担当させてあげてください). A favour coming to me takes いただく or くださる.
担当してもよろしいでしょうか asks permission for my own action, but then the doer is 私が, not 私に. 私に only works with the causative 〜させる.
tell: I want to do it, you must permit: 私に〜させていただけないでしょうか.

s: では、明日の午後2時に、私が御社に（　　）。
en: Then I will come to your office tomorrow at 2 p.m.
why: The action is mine (私が): going to the client's office. Humble language (謙譲): 伺う.
いらっしゃる is honorific (尊敬). It raises the doer, so it cannot describe my own visit.
おいでになる is also honorific. Never use it for yourself.
お越しになる is honorific for someone else's coming. My own visit needs humble language.
tell: My action → 謙譲 (伺う・参る). Their action → 尊敬 (いらっしゃる・お越しになる).

s: 先生が来週の学会で（　　）資料を、事前に拝見してもよろしいでしょうか。
en: May I see, in advance, the materials you will be using at next week's conference?
why: 先生が is the doer, so use honorific language (尊敬): お〜になる.
お〜する is humble (謙譲), for my own actions. The professor is the one using the materials.
使わせていただく means I use something with permission. The professor is the user.
お〜いただく means I receive the favour of someone using it. Its subject is the receiver, so it cannot follow 先生が.
tell: Xが + their action → お〜になる. お〜する and させていただく are for your own actions.

s: それでは、本日の講師をご紹介します。山本先生は、長年、海外で日本語教育に携わって（　　）。
en: Now let me introduce today's speaker. Professor Yamamoto has worked in Japanese language teaching overseas for many years.
why: The host describes the guest speaker's career to the audience, so honorific: 〜ていらっしゃる (尊敬 of いる).
おる is humble (謙譲). It is for yourself or your own side, not an honoured guest.
参る is humble for going or coming, and it would lower the guest.
〜ていただく means someone did the speaker a favour. Teaching overseas for years was not a favour to the host.
tell: Introducing a guest's career → 尊敬 〜ていらっしゃる. おる and 参る are for your own side.

s: お電話ありがとうございます。あいにく部長の田中は、ただいま会議に（　　）。終わり次第、こちらからお電話いたします。
en: Thank you for calling. I'm afraid our manager, Tanaka, is in a meeting right now. We will call you back as soon as it finishes.
c: 出ていらっしゃいます
why: To an outside caller, your own company counts as 'my side', so your own boss gets humble おる. 部長の田中 (no title after the name, no さん) shows this.
いらっしゃる raises the boss in front of an outsider. To people outside the company, your own staff take humble forms.
おいでだ is honorific and has the same problem.
〜られる is honorific too. Your own boss is lowered, not raised, when you speak to a client.
cue: お電話ありがとうございます
tell: To outsiders, your own company's people count as 'me': 部長の田中は〜ております.

s: 本日は誠に勝手ながら、店内改装のため、午後6時で閉店（　　）。
en: We apologise for the inconvenience, but today we will close at 6 p.m. for store renovations.
why: Closing is the shop's own action, done with the customers' indulgence. 〜させていただきます is the humble 'we will, with your leave'. 誠に勝手ながら sets this up.
〜していただきます means the customers will do the closing. Closing is the shop's action.
なさる is honorific for someone else's action. The shop cannot raise its own act.
〜てくださる means someone does it for us. Nobody closes the shop for the shop.
tell: Our own action, done with your leave (勝手ながら) → 〜させていただきます.

s: 先日、駅のホームで電車を待っていると、見知らぬ女性（　　）「このかばん、あなたのですか」と声をかけてきた。
en: The other day, while I was waiting for a train on the platform, a woman I had never seen before came up to me and asked, "Is this bag yours?"
why: 見知らぬ女性 enters the story for the first time. A new person or a new event in a story takes が.
は marks someone already known, or someone set against another person. This woman is a stranger who has only just appeared.
も means 'too' and needs someone else who also spoke to me. Nobody else has been mentioned.
なら takes up a topic someone has just raised (that woman? well, she…). Nobody has asked about her.
tell: Someone or something appears in the story for the first time → が. は is for what is already known.

s: 前の上司は細かいことまで指示する人だったが、今の上司（　　）部下に仕事を任せて、ほとんど口を出さない人だ。
en: My last boss told us what to do down to the smallest detail, but my current boss leaves the work to us and hardly ever interferes.
why: Two bosses are set side by side, and the second half says what kind of person the current one is. A contrast, and a description of someone already known, both take は.
が before 〜人だ singles the current boss out as 'the one who is like that', as if answering 'which boss?'. Nobody asked that.
も means 'also'. The previous boss was the opposite type, so 'also' contradicts the first half.
を marks the object of a verb. 今の上司 is the one who leaves the work to others, and 任せる already has its object, 仕事を.
tell: Aは…だが、B（ ）…: two things in contrast → は on both. が singles B out; も means 'the same'.

s: 今回の調査結果から判断すると、本計画は根本から見直さ（　　）と考える。
en: Judging from the results of this survey, we believe there is no choice but to rethink this plan from the ground up.
why: ざるを得ない is the written way to say 'have no choice but to'. 本計画 and 〜と考える mark a formal report in である style.
なきゃ is a spoken contraction of なければ. The meaning is close, but a written report cannot use it.
〜ないとまずい ('it'd be bad if we didn't') is casual speech. It does not belong in a report.
なくちゃ is a spoken contraction of なくては. A report needs the full written form.
tell: Formal report → no contractions: ざるを得ない (or なければならない), never なきゃ or なくちゃ.

s: 検討の結果、この方法は費用の面では決して効率的（　　）、安全性の高さを考えれば採用する価値があると判断した。
en: After review, we concluded that although this method is by no means cost-efficient, its high level of safety makes it worth adopting.
why: では + ない + が keeps every piece in written style. 検討の結果 and 判断した mark a formal report.
じゃ is the spoken contraction of では. Even with が after it, a report cannot use it.
けど is spoken. In formal writing the contrast takes が (or けれども).
Both じゃ and けど are spoken, so this is the fully casual version.
tell: Formal report → check every piece: では not じゃ, が not けど. One spoken bit spoils it.
